column1: What is SAP's core architectural invariant that distinguishes it from loosely-coupled microservices systems?
column2: Data consistency is enforced as a database-level invariant via ACID transactions in a single shared relational database, not as a procedural business rule across eventually-consistent services—trading horizontal scalability for transactional correctness.

column1: In SAP's three-tier architecture, what are the three distinct server process layers and what does each independently scale?
column2: Presentation (UI concurrency), Application processing (business logic throughput), and Database persistence (I/O capacity)—each separated into distinct server processes for independent scaling.

column1: What is the SAP 'client concept' and what does it guarantee?
column2: A mechanism that partitions a single physical database instance into logically isolated tenants, allowing one system to serve multiple legal entities while enforcing complete data segregation at the database query level.

column1: What is the 'synchronous integration post' invariant in SAP's core module architecture?
column2: When a business event occurs (e.g., a goods receipt in Materials Management), the corresponding financial document in Financial Accounting is created within the SAME database transaction, not via a subsequent batch run—eliminating batch reconciliation latency.

column1: Why is SAP master data (e.g., the material master) described as 'singular and authoritative'?
column2: A material master is one record with multiple module-specific views (accounting, warehouse, sales) under a single material number. All modules read from this one authoritative record, so an error in it propagates simultaneously to every downstream function—making master data governance a business control, not just IT housekeeping.

column1: In ABAP's architecture, why are background threads and function pointers prohibited, and what is used instead for inter-system communication?
column2: This stems from mainframe-heritage constraints (stateless dialog work processes for aggressive hardware multiplexing); inter-system communication instead relies on synchronous Remote Function Calls (RFCs).

column1: What is the ABAP Data Dictionary and what is the architectural trade-off of its metadata-driven design?
column2: A central metadata repository where fields inherit length, type, validation rules, and multilingual text labels from domains (e.g., MATNR). Trade-off: enables zero-code internationalization but imposes runtime overhead since every field access triggers a metadata lookup.

column1: What is an IDoc and why was it designed as asynchronous rather than synchronous messaging?
column2: An Intermediate Document is a structured, self-describing message envelope (header, control record, data segments) for exchanging business data. It was designed asynchronous because 1990s networks were unreliable and synchronous RFCs were prohibitively expensive—enabling queuing, retry, and audit without requiring sender and receiver to be online simultaneously.

column1: What role does the 'logical system' concept play in ALE (Application Link Enabling)?
column2: It creates a layer of indirection: the sending application issues an IDoc to a logical destination name rather than needing to know the receiving system's actual IP address or RFC connection details.

column1: What three mechanisms underlie SAP HANA's architectural inversion of the traditional disk-optimized database paradigm?
column2: (1) Columnar storage with high compression ratios (10:1 or better), (2) in-memory residency of the entire transactional database, and (3) massive query parallelization across multi-core CPUs—collapsing transactional and analytical processing into one unified platform.

column1: In BTP's clean-core extension strategy, what is the 'only coupling' permitted between an extension and the S/4HANA backend?
column2: The API boundary—extensions must consume only published OData services, REST endpoints, and events; direct dependency on an unexposed backend database table violates the contract.

column1: What is the difference between tenant isolation enforced by infrastructure vs. by application layer in BTP multi-tenancy?
column2: Infrastructure-level isolation uses separate HANA HDI containers per tenant (not just a tenant-ID column filter); application-level isolation is verified via tenant-aware JWT validation—both are required as a security/compliance boundary, not merely a performance preference.
